# Transfer Portal

> **Two source classes on this page, never mixed in one claim.** *How the guide defines it*, *how the guide uses it* and every page reference are **GUIDE CONTENT**. *Working definition*, *why it matters* and any arithmetic over printed figures are **TTW DERIVED** — this library's words, supplied because the guide supplies none. Where the guide neither defines nor develops a concept, the field reads `Not addressed in guide.` and is not padded out.

> Appears on **170 pages** of 345. A high count usually means the concept is woven through the 138 team tables, not that the guide discusses it that often — this is a count of locations, not of emphasis.

## How the guide defines it

Not addressed in guide.

## How the guide uses it

On 170 pages and treated as a first-order roster mechanism rather than a novelty. Contributors argue about whether it makes continuity obsolete — John McKechnie states outright that roster continuity is overrated in this era because elite teams reload on the fly — while others treat a portal class as the reason a team will collapse. Whole bets rest on it: UCLA's 'about 18 starting players filling spots', Penn State's 24 arrivals from Iowa State.

## Working definition — TTW DERIVED

The mechanism by which players transfer between programmes, and by extension a team's ability to rebuild a roster in one offseason.

## Why it matters — TTW DERIVED

It is the concept most actively contested inside the guide. It cuts against returning production as a projection input, and the guide does not settle which wins.

## How bettors use it in this guide

As evidence in both directions. A large portal haul supports an Over for UNLV and UCLA; a portal exodus supports an Under for North Texas and Southern Miss. Contributors also grade portal *management* as a programme skill, crediting Miami specifically.

pp. 22–27 and pp. 5–15 for the arguments; every team page for the arrivals and departures.
